c.tagline: Half the world — Persia's city of turquoise domes and grand squares.

taxi.fareNote: The Snapp and Tapsi apps give fixed fares. Foreign bank cards don't work in Iran, so pay taxis in cash (rials); app wallets are topped up with cash. Agree a fare before boarding shared or street taxis.

emergency.note: Fire: 125. English-speaking operators are not guaranteed; hotel staff can assist.

avoid.reason: Beware overly friendly 'plainclothes police' or money-exchange scams asking to see your passport or cash — real police rarely stop tourists.

hood_desc: The monumental heart of Isfahan around the UNESCO-listed Naqsh-e Jahan (Imam) Square, ringed by the Imam Mosque, Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, Ali Qapu Palace and the grand bazaar; the essential base for sightseeing on foot.
The historic Safavid promenade and modern spine of the city, a tree-lined avenue of shops, hotels, cafes and the Chahar Bagh School; central and lively, walkable to most of the main sights.

Isfahan's atmospheric New Julfa district, settled by Armenians in the 17th century and home to the frescoed Vank Cathedral and the city's trendiest cafes, galleries and boutiques; a relaxed, arty neighborhood.
The green riverside belt along the Zayandeh River and its celebrated Safavid bridges, Si-o-se-pol and Khaju, where locals stroll and picnic; a calm, scenic area a short walk from downtown.

The sprawling covered bazaar running north from Naqsh-e Jahan Square through the Qeysarie Gate, a warren of coppersmiths, carpet, spice and handicraft stalls; the place to stay for shopping and local buzz.

water.note: Tap water is generally treated and drinkable, but drought has affected quality and many prefer bottled.

transit.pay: Fares are paid with a rechargeable transit smart card tapped at metro gates and on buses; cash is generally not accepted on board. Single low fares make the metro and BRT the cheapest way to cross the city.
transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM, with buses and BRT on similar daytime hours; there is no overnight service, so late-night travelers rely on Snapp or Tapsi.
transit.note: Isfahan has a growing north-south metro (Line 1), a BRT busway and an extensive city bus network; women-only carriages are available on the metro. Snapp and Tapsi ride-hailing cover door-to-door trips.

tip.r: Rounding up is appreciated in taxis and restaurants; upscale hotels and restaurants may add a service charge. Not deeply ingrained but increasingly common in tourist-facing venues.

food.name: Beryani
food.desc: Isfahan's own dish: minced lamb cooked on a flat iron pan with cinnamon and spices, folded into taftoon bread with walnuts and mint.

places.name: Beryani Azam
places.note: Founded in 1916 and now the city's benchmark for beryani, with several branches.

places.name: Shahrzad Restaurant
places.note: Elegant 1960s dining room with stained glass; classic beryani and Persian stews.

places.name: Beryani Haj Mahmoud Shafiei
places.note: Old bazaar-side beryani counter, busy at lunch with Isfahani regulars.

food.name: Khoresh-e mast
food.desc: Isfahan's sweet-savoury yoghurt dish with saffron, sugar and shredded lamb or chicken, served chilled as a side or dessert.

places.name: Shahrzad Restaurant
places.note: The address most often named for khoresh-e mast done the traditional way.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Tiled courtyard restaurant on the great square; full Isfahani menu.

places.name: Shahrzad Esfahani
places.note: Traditional decor and live music with Isfahani specialities on the menu.

food.name: Fesenjan
food.desc: Rich stew of ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses with chicken or duck, dark, sour-sweet and served over saffron rice.

places.name: Shahrzad Restaurant
places.note: Long-established kitchen with a deep list of Persian khoresh.

places.name: Malek Soltan Jarchibashi
places.note: Restaurant set inside a restored Safavid bathhouse; striking room, classic stews.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Reliable stews and kebabs with a view onto the square's arcades.

food.name: Dizi (abgoosht)
food.desc: Lamb, chickpeas and potato slow-cooked in a stone crock; you drink the broth first, then mash the solids and eat them with bread.

places.name: Azadegan Teahouse
places.note: Cluttered, lamp-hung teahouse off the square; dizi and tea in the old style.

places.name: Malek Soltan Jarchibashi
places.note: Bathhouse setting makes it the most atmospheric place for a dizi lunch.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Dizi served with the full set of pickles, herbs and flatbread.

food.name: Kaleh joosh
food.desc: Thick Isfahani soup of dried whey with walnuts, mint, onion and turmeric, poured over torn bread - a winter-market dish.

places.name: Azadegan Teahouse
places.note: One of the few places still serving the old whey soups to visitors.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Isfahani starters including whey and herb soups.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg food stalls
places.note: Small bazaar kitchens serving ash and kaleh joosh to traders at midday.

food.name: Gaz nougat
food.desc: Isfahan's famous nougat made from the sap of the angebin plant with rosewater and pistachio or almond, sold in tins by the kilo.

places.name: Kermani Gaz
places.note: Well-known Isfahan gaz maker; tasting before buying is expected.

places.name: Sekkeh Gaz
places.note: Long-standing brand with shops around town and airport-safe packaging.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg confectioners
places.note: Rows of sweet shops selling gaz, poolaki and sohan; haggling is normal.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink, often carbonated and flecked with dried mint - the standard partner to kebab and beryani. No alcohol is served in Iran.

places.name: Beryani Azam
places.note: Chilled doogh is the automatic order alongside a beryani plate here.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: House doogh served in clay cups with the traditional menu.

places.name: Malek Soltan Jarchibashi
places.note: Doogh and non-alcoholic malt drinks with the bathhouse-restaurant meals.

food.name: Sharbat and Persian chai
food.desc: Cordials of saffron, bidmeshk willow blossom, rosewater or sekanjabin over ice, and strong black tea taken with rock sugar.

places.name: Azadegan Teahouse
places.note: Classic Isfahan chai house; tea, qalyan-free corners and cheap sweets.

places.name: Bastani Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Saffron and rosewater sharbats poured through the afternoon.

places.name: Si-o-se Pol teahouses
places.note: Teahouses under and beside the historic bridges, best at sunset.

landmarks: Naqsh-e Jahan Square (Imam Square)
A UNESCO-listed royal plaza among the world's largest, ringed by mosques, palaces and bazaars that embody the maxim 'Isfahan is half the world.'
Shah Mosque (Masjed-e Imam)
The crescendo of Safavid architecture, its turquoise dome and seven-color tilework creating echoing perfection at the square's southern end.
Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque
A private royal chapel whose cream-colored dome shifts hue with the sun, concealing perhaps the most sublime tiled interior in Islam.
Si-o-se-pol Bridge (Bridge of 33 Arches)
Isfahan's beloved double-decked Safavid bridge, whose 33 illuminated arches over the Zayandeh River draw evening strollers and singers.
Khaju Bridge
A 17th-century bridge-cum-weir with pavilioned alcoves where locals gather at dusk to chat and sing beneath vaulted arches.
Ali Qapu Palace
The Safavid shahs' towering gateway palace, its lofty terrace overlooking Imam Square and its music room carved with instrument-shaped niches.
Jameh Mosque of Isfahan (Friday Mosque)
A UNESCO-listed encyclopedia of twelve centuries of Iranian mosque architecture, from Seljuk brick domes to Safavid tiled iwans.
Chehel Sotoun Palace (Palace of Forty Columns)
A garden pavilion whose twenty slender columns double in its reflecting pool, sheltering vivid frescoes of Safavid banquets and battles.
Vank Cathedral (Holy Savior Cathedral)
The jewel of the Armenian quarter of New Julfa, blending Islamic domes with gilded frescoes of startling, vivid intensity.
Grand Bazaar of Isfahan and Qeysarie Gate
A vaulted labyrinth of carpets, miniatures and hammered copper linking Imam Square to the Friday Mosque through centuries of commerce.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international trains from Isfahan - Iran's only cross-border passenger services run from Tabriz and Mashhad. Isfahan station is south of the city, with overnight trains to Tehran taking about 7 hours and services to Shiraz, Yazd and Mashhad. Raja's site is Persian-language and foreign cards do not work, so most visitors book through a hotel or local agent.

bus.note: No international coaches from Isfahan itself - they run from Tehran and Tabriz. The Kaveh terminal in the north is the main hub, with comfortable VIP coaches to Tehran (about 5-6 hours), Shiraz (7), Yazd (4) and Kashan (2-3) on Seiro Safar and Hamsafar. Buy at the terminal, in cash; carry rials as foreign cards do not work anywhere in Iran.

ferry.note: Isfahan is on the central Iranian plateau with no navigable water - the Zayandeh Rud river through the city is often dry - so there are no ferries. Iran's passenger boats run from the Persian Gulf ports at Bandar Abbas to Qeshm and Kish.

half.name: Nain
half.blurb: A desert town midway to Yazd with one of Iran's oldest surviving mosques, about two hours from Isfahan.

half.name: Varzaneh
half.blurb: A small desert town with sand dunes, a salt lake, and traditional pigeon towers, about ninety minutes from Isfahan.

full.name: Kashan
full.blurb: A desert city of restored merchant courtyard houses and the Fin Garden, about two and a half hours from Isfahan.

full.name: Abyaneh
full.blurb: A red-clay hillside village with mudbrick houses and traditions dating back some 1,500 years, roughly three hours from Isfahan.
